steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on contextual bandits where a revealer with a limited budget decides when to reveal patient information to a recommender, motivated by digital health. Include the motivation, our contributions, and related work.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: pro-treatment actions in digital health and costly nudges
- Research question and the two-agent (recommender / revealer) reformulation
- Commercial sensor example
## Our Contributions
- Algorithm for timing the revealer's actions; decomposition into two parts
- Guarantees: competitive ratio and sublinear regret
## Related Work
- Online optimization algorithms
- Contextual bandits under resource constraints
- Contextual bandits with delayed feedback

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Pro-treatment actions in digital health
  - patients asked to take actions with no immediate benefit to them, needed for treatment effectiveness -> call them pro-treatment actions
  - e.g. personalized addiction treatment: effectiveness compromised if patients fail to complete self-reports (cite)
  - second scenario: commercial sensors, or aggregating data across multiple patients
  - sensor data only accessible via cloud servers; data-collecting device (wearables, electronic toothbrush) may only talk to intervention-delivery device (smartphones) through the cloud
  - patients may need to open a dedicated app so it retrieves latest treatment recommendations from the cloud (cite)
  - when patients neglect these actions: clinicians resort to limited, costly nudges, e.g. clinician follow-ups
- Question + reformulation
  - given limited budget for expensive nudges when patients fail to take pro-treatment actions, when to use them?
  - two agents
  - recommender: learning agent, uses all revealed patient info up to current time to recommend treatment action for next time step
  - revealer: has current (or surrogate of current) and past patient data, often from sensors; decides whether to reveal it to recommender -> enables learning personalized treatment
- Commercial sensor example
  - recommendations (smart phone notifications) often made by cloud-based RL algorithm
  - RL algorithm observes everything up to current time, but recommendations hidden unless patient opens the app (pro-treatment action)
  - clinician = revealer, prompts patient to open app (Figure 1; assume patient never opens it on their own)
  - at decision points clinician assesses all sensor data, decides whether to contact patient
  - patient opens app -> gets most recent recommended notification; otherwise "outdated" recommendation based on info up to last reveal
  - equivalently: recommender only has history up to last reveal; opening the app gives it the whole sensor data history
## Our Contributions
- Algorithm for "optimal" timing of revealer's actions, limited number of actions
  - special case: recommender = linear contextual bandit when revealer reveals; multi-armed bandit (MAB) when nothing revealed (missing context)
  - decomposition: 1) online primal-dual optimization algorithm (revealer's decision); 2) contextual bandit learning with delayed feedback (recommender's decision)
- Guarantees
  - novel learning constraint in online primal-dual algorithm
  - Algorithm 1: objective value at least \pi_{\min}(1-1/c) times offline clairvoyant benchmark; \pi_{\min} problem dependent constant; 1-1/c budget dependent, approaches 1-1/e as budget grows
  - learning constraint separates out effect of delayed feedback in bandit learning loss (§ 2) -> no dependency on context dimension
  - combined: first UCB-based algorithm (Algorithm 2) with sublinear regret under suitable parameters
## Related Work
- three streams: (i) online optimization algorithms, (ii) contextual bandits under resource constraints, (iii) contextual bandits with delayed feedback
- (i): two arrival settings, stochastic and adversarial
  - stochastic: forecasted arrival pattern from historical data or stochastic arrival assumption (cite)
  - adversarial: robust to changes in arrival pattern (cite)
  - online primal-dual mechanism: uses dual program to guide online decisions (cite)
  - ours: new class of online primal-dual mechanisms with learning component, used as online allocation sub-routine
  - evaluated by competitive ratio vs clairvoyant policy on worst-case input
- (ii): each action consumes resources
  - online algorithms for standard MAB (cite), contextual bandit and other RL methods (cite)

  - ours: structured delays, no new info unless revealer acts

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In digital health, patients are often asked to take actions that do not give them any immediate benefit but that are needed for the treatments to be effective. We call these actions pro-treatment actions. One example is personalized addiction treatment, where the treatment may not be as effective if patients do not complete their self-reports. Another scenario is when commercial sensors are used, or when data has to be aggregated across multiple patients. In this case the data from the sensor can only be accessed through cloud servers, which means that the device collecting the data, for example wearables or an electronic toothbrush, may only be able to communicate with the device delivering the intervention, for example a smartphone, through the cloud. So to make sure personalized treatments are delivered properly, patients may need to open a dedicated app on their smartphones, so that the app can get the latest treatment recommendations from the cloud. When patients neglect pro-treatment actions, clinicians may use nudges to encourage compliance, such as clinician follow-ups, but these nudges are limited and costly.

The question we want to answer is the following: if there is a limited budget of expensive nudges to use when patients fail to take pro-treatment actions, when should the nudges be used? To answer it we reformulate the problem with two agents. The first agent is a recommender. It is a learning agent that uses all the patient information revealed up to the current time to recommend the treatment action for the next time step. The second agent is a revealer. The revealer has the current (or some surrogate of the current) and the past patient data, which is often collected by sensors, and it decides whether to reveal this information to the recommender, so that personalized treatment can be learned.

Going back to the commercial sensor example, the recommendations (smart phone notifications) are often made by a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm running in the cloud. The RL algorithm observes all the information up to the current time, but these up-to-date recommendations stay hidden from the patient unless the patient opens a dedicated app on the phone, which is the pro-treatment action. The clinician is the revealer here, and prompts the patient to open the app as a way to reveal information (Figure 1 shows this, assuming that the patient never opens the app on their own). At decision points the clinician looks at all the sensor data and decides whether to contact the patient or not. If the clinician contacts the patient and the patient opens the mobile application, they receives the most recent recommended notification. If not, the patient gets an "outdated" recommendation that is based on the information up to the last reveal. So equivalently, in this problem the recommender only has access to the history up to the last reveal, but when the app is opened the recommender gets access to the whole sensor data history.

## Our Contributions

In this work we give an algorithm that decides the "optimal" timing for the revealer to act when the number of actions it can take is limited. We look at the special case where the recommender acts 1) as a linear contextual bandit algorithm when the revealer chooses to reveal information and 2) as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithm when no additional information is revealed to the recommender, because the context is missing. We show that the problem can be decomposed into two parts: 1) an online primal-dual optimization algorithm, which handles the decision of the revealer, and 2) a contextual bandit learning algorithm with delayed feedback, which models the decision of the recommender.

- Guarantees
  - novel learning constraint in online primal-dual algorithm
  - Algorithm 1: objective value at least \pi_{\min}(1-1/c) times offline clairvoyant benchmark; \pi_{\min} problem dependent constant; 1-1/c budget dependent, approaches 1-1/e as budget grows
  - learning constraint separates out effect of delayed feedback in bandit learning loss (§ 2) -> no dependency on context dimension
  - combined: first UCB-based algorithm (Algorithm 2) with sublinear regret under suitable parameters

## Related Work
- three streams: (i) online optimization algorithms, (ii) contextual bandits under resource constraints, (iii) contextual bandits with delayed feedback
- (i): two arrival settings, stochastic and adversarial
  - stochastic: forecasted arrival pattern from historical data or stochastic arrival assumption (cite)
  - adversarial: robust to changes in arrival pattern (cite)
  - online primal-dual mechanism: uses dual program to guide online decisions (cite)
  - ours: new class of online primal-dual mechanisms with learning component, used as online allocation sub-routine
  - evaluated by competitive ratio vs clairvoyant policy on worst-case input

- (ii): each action consumes resources
  - online algorithms for standard MAB (cite), contextual bandit and other RL methods (cite)
  - ours: recommender must act at every time step whether or not it observes current context
  - a few works: Thompson sampling + online optimization for contextual bandit with resource constraints (cite)
  - ours: first analysis for UCB-based algorithms; learning inside online allocation mechanism (theirs: learning only in bandit part) -> better performance

- (iii): delayed feedback in MAB (cite) and contextual bandit (cite); bounded or stochastic delays
  - ours: structured delays, no new info unless revealer acts
  - applying (iii) algorithms feasible, but ours has much stronger guarantee
  - regret order tight (optimal) up to logarithmic factor (cite)
  - delayed feedback adds only \sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{t}, order \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})
  - unlike two earlier works (cite, cite): no dependency of delay effect on context dimension d

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In digital health, patients are often asked to take actions that do not give them any immediate benefit but that are needed for the treatments to be effective. We call these actions pro-treatment actions. One example is personalized addiction treatment, where the treatment may not be as effective if patients do not complete their self-reports. Another scenario is when commercial sensors are used, or when data has to be aggregated across multiple patients. In this case the data from the sensor can only be accessed through cloud servers, which means that the device collecting the data, for example wearables or an electronic toothbrush, may only be able to communicate with the device delivering the intervention, for example a smartphone, through the cloud. So to make sure personalized treatments are delivered properly, patients may need to open a dedicated app on their smartphones, so that the app can get the latest treatment recommendations from the cloud. When patients neglect pro-treatment actions, clinicians may use nudges to encourage compliance, such as clinician follow-ups, but these nudges are limited and costly.

The question we want to answer is the following: if there is a limited budget of expensive nudges to use when patients fail to take pro-treatment actions, when should the nudges be used? To answer it we reformulate the problem with two agents. The first agent is a recommender. It is a learning agent that uses all the patient information revealed up to the current time to recommend the treatment action for the next time step. The second agent is a revealer. The revealer has the current (or some surrogate of the current) and the past patient data, which is often collected by sensors, and it decides whether to reveal this information to the recommender, so that personalized treatment can be learned.

Going back to the commercial sensor example, the recommendations (smart phone notifications) are often made by a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm running in the cloud. The RL algorithm observes all the information up to the current time, but these up-to-date recommendations stay hidden from the patient unless the patient opens a dedicated app on the phone, which is the pro-treatment action. The clinician is the revealer here, and prompts the patient to open the app as a way to reveal information (Figure 1 shows this, assuming that the patient never opens the app on their own). At decision points the clinician looks at all the sensor data and decides whether to contact the patient or not. If the clinician contacts the patient and the patient opens the mobile application, they receives the most recent recommended notification. If not, the patient gets an "outdated" recommendation that is based on the information up to the last reveal. So equivalently, in this problem the recommender only has access to the history up to the last reveal, but when the app is opened the recommender gets access to the whole sensor data history.

## Our Contributions

In this work we give an algorithm that decides the "optimal" timing for the revealer to act when the number of actions it can take is limited. We look at the special case where the recommender acts 1) as a linear contextual bandit algorithm when the revealer chooses to reveal information and 2) as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithm when no additional information is revealed to the recommender, because the context is missing. We show that the problem can be decomposed into two parts: 1) an online primal-dual optimization algorithm, which handles the decision of the revealer, and 2) a contextual bandit learning algorithm with delayed feedback, which models the decision of the recommender.

In the online primal-dual algorithm we introduce a novel learning constraint. We prove that the objective function value of our proposed algorithm, Algorithm 1, is at least \pi_{\min}(1-1/c) times the value of an offline clairvoyant benchmark. Here \pi_{\min} is a problem dependent constant and 1-1/c is a budget dependent constant that approaches 1-1/e as the budget grows. Also, because of the novel learning constraint in the primal-dual algorithm, we can separate out the effect of delayed feedback in the bandit learning loss (defined in § 2), and this removes the dependency of the delayed feedback effect on the context dimension. Putting the two parts together, we give the first UCB-based algorithm (Algorithm 2) that gets a sublinear regret when the parameters are chosen suitably.

## Related Work

Our work is related to three streams of literature: (i) online optimization algorithms, (ii) contextual bandits under resource constraints, and (iii) contextual bandits with delayed feedback. Studies in (i) usually look at two arrival settings, stochastic and adversarial. In the stochastic setting, online algorithms either use an arrival pattern forecasted from historical data or they assume a stochastic arrival pattern. In the adversarial setting, the algorithms are robust to possible changes in the arrival pattern. The online primal-dual mechanism is one class of algorithms, which uses the dual program to guide the decisions of the online algorithm. In our work we introduce a new class of online primal-dual mechanisms that has a learning component, and we use it as an online allocation sub-routine in our framework. We evaluate its performance with a competitive ratio, which compares it to a clairvoyant policy on the worst-case input instance.

Studies in (ii) usually assume that every action consumes some amount of resources. Under these resource constraints, earlier works proposed online algorithms for standard MAB, contextual bandit, and other RL methods. In our algorithm, on the other hand, the recommender has to take an action at every time step, whether it observes the current context or not. A few works formulate contextual bandit with resource constraints by combining Thompson sampling (bandit) algorithms with online optimization algorithms. Compared to them, our work gives the first analysis for UCB-based bandit algorithms, and we put a learning component into the online allocation mechanisms, while in their algorithms learning only happens in the bandit part. This extra level of learning helps our algorithms perform better.

Studies in (iii) include delayed feedback both in MAB and in contextual bandit, and the delay patterns are mostly bounded delays or stochastic delays. In our problem, though, the delay patterns are structured: the recommender gets no additional information unless the revealer takes an action. It is feasible to apply algorithms from (iii) to our problem setting, but our algorithm has a much stronger theoretical guarantee. Our regret bound is tight (optimal) in order up to a logarithmic factor. Also, the delayed feedback only affects our regret bound through an additive factor of \sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{t}, which is of order \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}). So unlike the results of one earlier work and of another, our theoretical result removes the dependency of the delayed feedback effect on the context dimension d.

steps.text:
In digital health, to ensure the effectiveness of treatments, patients are often asked to take actions that have no immediate benefit to them. We refer to these as pro-treatment actions. For instance, in personalized addiction treatment, the effectiveness of the treatment may be compromised if patients fail to complete self-reports [1]. Another scenario arises when commercial sensors are used or when data must be aggregated across multiple patients. In this case, sensor data can only be accessed via cloud servers, so the data-collecting device, such as wearables and electronic toothbrush, may only be able to communicate with the intervention-delivery device, such as smartphones, through the cloud. To ensure that personalized treatments are delivered properly, patients may need to open a dedicated app on their smartphones, enabling the app to retrieve the latest treatment recommendations from the cloud [2]. When patients neglect pro-treatment actions, clinicians may resort to limited, costly nudges, such as clinician follow-ups, to encourage compliance.

We are interested in the following question: given a limited budget for expensive nudges to be used when patients fail to take pro-treatment actions, when should these nudges be used? To answer this question, we reformulate the problem with two agents. The first agent is a recommender, specifically a learning agent that uses all the revealed patient information up to the current time to recommend the treatment action for the next time step. The second agent, a revealer, has current (or some surrogate of current) and past patient data, often collected by sensors, and determines whether to reveal this information to the recommender, which enables the learning of personalized treatment.

In the commercial sensor example, the recommendations (smart phone notifications) are often made by a cloud-based reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm. Although the RL algorithm observes all the information up to the current time, these up-to-date recommendations stay hidden from the patient unless they open a dedicated app on their phone (i.e., take a pro-treatment action). The clinician serves as the revealer, prompting the patient to open the app as a way of revealing information (see Figure 1, assuming the patient never opens the app on their own). At decision points, the clinician assesses all sensor data and decides whether to contact the patient. If the clinician contacts the patient and the patient opens the mobile application, they receives the most recent recommended notification. Otherwise, the patient receives an "outdated" recommendation based on the information up to the last reveal. Equivalently, the recommender in this problem only has access to the history up to the last reveal, but upon opening the app it gains access to the entire sensor data history.

## Our Contributions

In this work, we provide an algorithm for deciding the "optimal" timing of the revealer's actions when the number of actions it can take is limited. We focus on the special case where the recommender acts 1) as a linear contextual bandit algorithm when the revealer opts to reveal information and 2) as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithm when no additional information is revealed to the recommender (due to the missing context). We show that the problem decomposes into two parts: 1) an online primal-dual optimization algorithm that addresses the decision of the revealer, and 2) a contextual bandit learning algorithm with delayed feedback that models the decision of the recommender.

In the online primal-dual algorithm, we introduce a novel learning constraint and prove that the objective value of our proposed algorithm, Algorithm 1, is at least \pi_{\min}(1-1/c) times that of an offline clairvoyant benchmark, where \pi_{\min} is a problem dependent constant and 1-1/c is a budget dependent constant approaching 1-1/e as the budget grows. In addition, the novel learning constraint lets us separate out the effect of delayed feedback in the bandit learning loss (defined in § 2), which removes the dependency of the delayed feedback effect on the context dimension. Combining the two parts, we provide the first UCB-based algorithm (Algorithm 2) that achieves sublinear regret under a suitable choice of parameters.

## Related Work

Our work is related to three streams of literature: (i) online optimization algorithms, (ii) contextual bandits under resource constraints, and (iii) contextual bandits with delayed feedback. Studies in (i) typically consider two arrival settings: stochastic and adversarial. In the stochastic setting, online algorithms either rely on an arrival pattern forecasted from historical data or assume a stochastic arrival pattern [3,4,5,6,7,8,9], whereas in the adversarial setting, algorithms are robust to possible changes in the arrival pattern [10,11,12,13,14,15,16]. The online primal-dual mechanism is a class of algorithms that leverages the dual program to guide the decisions of the online algorithm [17,13]. In our work, we introduce a new class of online primal-dual mechanisms with a learning component and use it as an online allocation sub-routine in our proposed framework. We evaluate its performance using a competitive ratio, which compares it to a clairvoyant policy on the worst-case input instance.

Studies in (ii) usually assume that each action consumes a certain amount of resources. Under such constraints, previous works have proposed online algorithms for standard MAB [18,19,20], contextual bandit, and other RL methods [21,22,23,24,25,26]. In contrast, the recommender in our algorithm must take an action at each time step regardless of whether it observes the current context. A few works formulate contextual bandit with resource constraints by integrating Thompson sampling (bandit) algorithms with online optimization algorithms [27,14]. In comparison, our work provides the first analysis for UCB-based bandit algorithms, and we incorporate a learning component into the online allocation mechanisms, whereas learning only happens in the bandit part of their algorithms. This additional level of learning helps our algorithms achieve better performance.

Studies in (iii) include delayed feedback in both MAB [28,29,30] and contextual bandit [31,32,33], where the delay patterns are mostly bounded or stochastic. In our problem, however, the delay patterns are structured: unless the revealer takes an action, the recommender receives no additional information. While it is feasible to apply algorithms from (iii) to our setting, our algorithm offers a significantly stronger theoretical guarantee. The order of our regret bound is tight (optimal) up to a logarithmic factor [34]. Moreover, the delayed feedback only affects our regret bound by an additive factor of \sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{t}, which is of order \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}). Therefore, unlike [31] and [32], our theoretical result removes the dependency of the delayed feedback effect on the context dimension d.
